name: Yara Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for your time, Yara. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think in private. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm lead carpenter for Hollis & Sons, a family builder in our town. We do new houses on the edge of town, barn conversions, a lot of roofs. I learned the trade from my dad, he was a carpenter forty years, and then did my apprenticeship with old Mr. Hollis. Most days I'm on site at seven, I've got three men and an apprentice under me, and we work till the light goes or the job's done.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love cutting a roof. Working out the rafters with a square and a pencil, the way my dad showed me, and seeing it all land right. People drive past a house I framed and they don't know it was me, but I know. What wears me out is the forms and the online stuff the council wants now. I don't use any of that AI business, never have, and I don't plan to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, that's what I'd have guessed. A lot of fuss over a gadget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've been saying: you can't build a house from a phone. It's for people in offices, and good luck to them. I wouldn't post anything, I'm not on that stuff much, but I'd say it at the pub after work, no doubt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad, and I'd thank God for it, honestly. I want to do this work my whole life, and I want my kids to see me do it. If nothing changes, that's the best news I could get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on just as I am. Mateo and I are getting married in the spring, and we've got my grandmother's plot of land at the edge of town, so the plan is to build our own house on it over the next few years, mostly with my own hands. I'd keep saving toward the materials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, really. Like hearing the rain's going to miss us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd build the house mostly with your own hands. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Weekends and evenings, for two or three years. Mateo's a mechanic, he's useless with a saw but he can dig a trench and carry timber all day. My dad would do the roof with me, he's already drawn it on the back of an envelope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work who'd be especially glad to hear this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Mr. Hollis, for sure. He's 70 and still comes to site in his boots. He'd say the same thing he says about everything new: it'll pass, like the last thing passed.

S0.say: You can't build a house from a phone, and AI is for people in offices. She wouldn't post online but would say it at the pub after work.
S0.think: She'd be glad and thank God for it, because she wants to do this work all her life and have her future children see her do it.
S0.do: Carries on as now, saving for materials to build her own house on her grandmother's plot after marrying Mateo in the spring, mostly with her own hands.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved, like rain that's going to miss them.
S0.quote: My dad would do the roof with me, he's already drawn it on the back of an envelope.
S0.fieldNote: Yara's identity is woven from family, faith and craft: her father's square and pencil, the old boss, the plot from her grandmother. Her resistance to technology is a matter of pride, not fear. This scenario confirms the life she already planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strong change but not a revolution. Hm. In the cities, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it'll hit the offices and the big firms, but small builders like us will carry on. People round here want someone they know building their house. I'd tell anyone that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be alright. Mr. Hollis won't buy robots, and his son Colin is the same. The thing that might bother me is if the council and the big suppliers make everything digital, so you can't get a permit or order timber without using some system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on working. If the paperwork side went all digital, I'd get Mateo or Colin to handle it for me rather than learn it. I'd wait and see what actually changes here before doing anything different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit irritated at the idea of more screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the young people coming into the trade only want to learn the new tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then they'd be missing out. My apprentice, Josh, is 18 and always on his phone, but I make him cut a set of stairs by hand before he's allowed near anything with a plug. He grumbles, but last month he did a perfect set and he was grinning all afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think would push these changes, if they came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big companies and people in the city who've never built a thing. They see a spreadsheet and think a house is just numbers. Out here, a house is where a family lives for fifty years.

S1.say: The change will hit offices and big firms, while small local builders carry on because people want someone they know building their house.
S1.think: She'd be alright, since her employer won't buy robots. Her concern is the council and suppliers making permits and ordering digital-only.
S1.do: Carries on working and hands any digital paperwork to Mateo or her boss's son rather than learning it. Waits to see what actually changes locally.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, a little irritated at the thought of more screens.
S1.quote: I make him cut a set of stairs by hand before he's allowed near anything with a plug.
S1.fieldNote: Yara trusts the small-town, family-firm world to protect her. She blames city people and big companies who see houses as numbers. Her pride in teaching her apprentice the hand way stands out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Lord. That's before we'd even get the house built.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to slow down and think about what they're doing to families. I don't believe in waiting for handouts, but I'd say companies have a duty to the people who built them. I'd be saying it at church and in town, I'm sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it scares me. If robots can cut a roof as well as me, then everything my dad taught me is worth nothing, and I've got nothing else, I never wanted anything else. I don't know how to start over with screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, Mateo and I would bring the wedding forward and get the house on the plot built as fast as we could, while I've still got work and wages to pay for materials. I'd stop spending on anything but the house. And I'd lean on family, my dad, Mateo's brothers, people from church, to help us build it on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake. I'd pray a lot, I know that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why build the house first, before anything else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a house with no mortgage is the one thing they can't take off you. If work goes, at least we've got a roof and a garden for vegetables. My grandmother lived through hard times on that same land, and that's what she'd have done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't believe in handouts. If government offered income support in this picture, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hate it. I'd probably take it for a bit if I really had to, to keep food on the table. But I'd be looking for any honest work at the same time, even outside building. I'd never just sit at home on it.

S2.say: People need to slow down and think about what this does to families, and companies have a duty to those who built them, though she doesn't believe in waiting for handouts.
S2.think: It scares her, because if robots can cut a roof, everything her father taught her is worthless and she has nothing else. She doesn't know how to start over with screens.
S2.do: Brings the wedding forward and builds the house on her grandmother's plot as fast as possible while she still earns. Cuts all spending except the house and leans on family and church to help build.
S2.quote: If robots can cut a roof as well as me, then everything my dad taught me is worth nothing, and I've got nothing else, I never wanted anything else.
S2.fieldNote: Her resistance to technology leaves her with no fallback, which is what alarms her. Her answer is very traditional: own the house outright, lean on family and faith. She'd reluctantly accept support, which she names as a contradiction with her own views.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit better. Enough to get the house up, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to plan, so let's keep apprenticeships going and look after local workers. I'd say the government should make sure our skills aren't just thrown away. Something like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is enough to get the house built and paid for, and that matters most to me. After that, I really don't know. I'd hope there's still some work for people who do it the proper way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd keep the wedding in the spring and build the house over three years instead of five. I'd put every spare bit into materials and work most weekends on it. Once the robots came, I'd keep working for Mr. Hollis as long as he'd have me, and pick up repair work on old buildings in the area.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Less than with two years, but still a knot in my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider learning any of the new tools in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe if Colin made me. I'm not proud of saying that, but it's the truth. I'd rather spend those evenings on my own roof than in front of a laptop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change your thinking about having children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We want kids, and that's not something I'd put off because of a machine. If anything, I'd want them to grow up seeing their mum and dad build something real with their hands.

S3.say: There's time to plan, so keep apprenticeships going, look after local workers and make sure skills aren't thrown away.
S3.think: Five years is enough to build and pay for the house, which matters most to her. After that she doesn't know, but hopes there's still work for people who do it the proper way.
S3.do: Keeps the spring wedding and speeds the house build from five years to three, putting spare money into materials. Stays with her employer and picks up repair work on old buildings once robots arrive.
S3.feel: Anxious, with a knot in her stomach, though less than with two years.
S3.quote: If anything, I'd want them to grow up seeing their mum and dad build something real with their hands.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time mostly goes into the same goal: a debt-free house. She openly admits she'd only learn new tools if forced. Her plans for children are firm and tied to her values about real work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. Kids at school, hopefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for people to adjust if they want to, and it's up to families and communities to look after each other. I'd say keep the apprenticeships going no matter what. That's what I'd tell people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine for most of it, house built, maybe kids, and still working. What worries me is the end of it, when I'm 37 with a family and the work dries up. But ten years is a long time and things don't always go the way people say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, build the house at a normal pace, save what we can. I'd probably take on a second apprentice to keep the trade going in town. I'd wait and see what's really happening by year seven or eight before changing anything big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd put it to the back of my mind most days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why take on another apprentice, if the work might disappear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because somebody has to know how to do it properly, whatever happens. If the robots break, or the power goes, someone needs to cut a roof by hand. I'd feel like I was keeping a light on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should look after people if work does dry up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first, then church and neighbours. That's how it's always been round here. If government has to help, fine, but it should be to keep people working, not to pay them to sit at home.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty for people who want to adjust, and families and communities should look after each other. Apprenticeships must continue no matter what.
S4.think: She'd be fine for most of the decade, with the house built and maybe children, but worries about the end when she'd be 37 with a family and less work.
S4.do: Keeps working, builds the house at a normal pace and saves. Takes on a second apprentice and waits until year seven or eight before any big change.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but mostly kept at the back of her mind.
S4.quote: If the robots break, or the power goes, someone needs to cut a roof by hand. I'd feel like I was keeping a light on.
S4.fieldNote: Given a decade, Yara chooses to pass on the craft rather than change it, taking on another apprentice. Her view of who should help is clear: family, church and neighbours first. Her unease is real but she keeps it at a distance.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd lose the trade before I could even finish our house. What would help is if building firms were made to keep apprenticeships and local crews going, and maybe help with costs for people building their own homes. Not a handout, help to keep working.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to small towns. Everyone talks about the cities. Out here, if the builder and the garage and the farm all go to robots, the whole town goes quiet.

headlineQuote: Because a house with no mortgage is the one thing they can't take off you.
portrait: Yara Costa is a 27-year-old lead carpenter for a small family builder in her town, taught by her father to cut roofs with a square and pencil, and firmly against AI tools. She plans to marry her mechanic fiancé Mateo in the spring and build their own house on her grandmother's plot. She is calm in the AI Plateau and Steady Disruption, trusting local loyalty, but the two-year AGI picture alarms her because she has nothing to fall back on. Across the AGI pictures her answer stays the same: build a debt-free house, lean on family and church, and keep apprenticeships alive.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she'd lose the trade before she could finish building her own house.
whatWouldHelp: Rules making building firms keep apprenticeships and local crews going, and help with costs for people building their own homes, as support to keep working rather than a handout.
